pages.h: How fast is it changing right now?
pages.html:
The slope of a straight line is rise over run. A curve has a different slope at every point, so measure it over a tiny run: pick two points h apart and compute (f(x+h) - f(x)) / h - the secant. As h shrinks the secant turns into the tangent, and the slope it settles on is the derivative f'(x).

lessons.title: Integrals, gradients and gradient descent
lessons.blurb: Area under a curve, the downhill arrow in 3-D, and the training loop.

pages.html:
An integral adds up infinitely many infinitely thin rectangles to get the area under a curve. With n rectangles of width w = (b - a) / n the area is about sum(f(x_i) * w); as n grows the sum closes in on the exact integral. Where the curve is below the axis the area counts negative.

This is an excerpt. The full lesson continues in the course.

pages.caption: The gradient is the uphill arrow; descent steps the other way. Try a learning rate of 1.2 to see it overshoot.
pages.html: Open it full screen with every control: Concept Explorer.

pages.caption: Move from and to, press More rectangles and watch the sum converge on the exact value. Try exp(-x^2) (the shape of the bell curve).

pages.h: The gradient: derivatives in many directions
pages.html:
With two inputs a function is a surface (a hill or a bowl). At every point the gradient (df/dx, df/dy) is the arrow pointing straight uphill; its length is the steepness. Gradient descent trains a model by repeating position = position - learning_rate * gradient: always step downhill. In deep learning the "surface" is the loss over millions of weights - same idea, many more dimensions.

This is an excerpt. The full lesson continues in the course.

pages.caption: Pick valley and press Descend: the red path zig-zags down a narrow valley. Raise the learning rate to 0.9 and watch it overshoot and bounce. Click the surface to start somewhere else. The same picture - with many more dimensions - is the loss landscape of a neural network.

lessons.title: Probability and Bayes: updating what you believe
lessons.blurb: Counting, simulating, and why a 95%-accurate test can be wrong most of the time.

pages.h: Probability is a number from 0 to 1
pages.html:
• Event: something that may happen. P(A) = favourable outcomes / all outcomes (when equally likely).
  • Independent events multiply: P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B). Exclusive events add: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).
  • Conditional: P(A | B) is the chance of A once you know B happened.
  • Bayes' rule: P(A | B) = P(B | A) x P(A) / P(B) - how to flip a conditional and update a belief.

This is an excerpt. The full lesson continues in the course.

lessons.title: Sampling, the bell curve and confidence intervals
lessons.blurb: Why averages are bell-shaped and how sure you can be from a sample.

pages.h: From a sample to the truth
pages.html:
You rarely see the whole population, only a sample. The sample mean wobbles from sample to sample, but the Central Limit Theorem says that the average of many samples is bell-shaped around the true mean whatever the population looks like, with spread sd / sqrt(n) (the standard error). A 95% confidence interval is mean +/- 1.96 x standard error: if you repeated the study many times, about 95 of 100 such intervals would contain the true mean.

This is an excerpt. The full lesson continues in the course.

pages.caption: Pick a skewed population (like incomes). Press Draw 500 samples: the histogram of sample means forms the orange bell even though the population is not bell-shaped. Raise n and the bell narrows by 1/sqrt(n). The green bar is the confidence interval from the last single sample.

lessons.title: Loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
lessons.blurb: How the weights learn: the gradient, the chain rule, the training loop.

pages.h: Learning = rolling downhill on the loss
pages.html:
The loss measures how wrong the predictions are (for classification: log-loss). It depends on every weight, so it is a surface: for two weights, a landscape in 3-D. Gradient descent computes the slope at the current weights and steps downhill: w = w - lr * gradient. Backpropagation is just the chain rule used to get all the slopes efficiently, working backwards from the loss to each layer.

This is an excerpt. The full lesson continues in the course.

pages.h: Gradient descent: a ball on the loss surface
pages.caption: The slope under the ball tells it which way is downhill. Change the learning rate and watch it crawl, glide or overshoot.
pages.html: Open it full screen with every control: Concept Explorer.

pages.caption: Slide the learning rate: 0.3 glides to the minimum, 0.95 zig-zags, above 1.0 the ball flies off the chart.
Real loss surfaces have valleys, ridges and several dips. Gradient descent is a ball rolling on this surface. Change the formula and rotate it.

pages.h: Every stage can fail - so measure every stage
pages.html:
• Chunk the documents (sentences, paragraphs or fixed windows with overlap). Too big: vectors blur many topics. Too small: no context.
  • Embed + index the chunks.
  • Retrieve top-k chunks (hybrid = keywords/BM25 + vectors; then rerank with a stronger model).
  • Generate with a prompt that contains the chunks and says "answer only from the context and cite the source; if it is not there, say you do not know".
  • Evaluate: hit-rate@k (is the right doc in the top k?), MRR (how high is it?), and answer faithfulness (does the answer match the context?).

lessons.title: GraphRAG: retrieval over a knowledge graph
lessons.blurb: Entities and relations, multi-hop questions, why graphs complement vectors.

pages.h: Vectors find similar passages; graphs follow relationships
pages.html:
Some questions need several facts joined together: "Which supplier of our best-selling product is based in a country with new export rules?" No single chunk contains the answer. GraphRAG extracts entities (nodes) and relations (edges) from the documents into a knowledge graph, then answers by walking the graph (neighbours, paths, communities) and giving those facts to the LLM. Microsoft's GraphRAG also summarises communities of nodes to answer "what are the main themes?" questions.

pages.h: A chatbot answers; an agent acts
pages.html:
An agent wraps an LLM in a loop: think (decide what to do), act (call a tool: search, database, calculator, an API), observe (read the result), repeat until it can answer. Tool calling (function calling) means the model outputs a structured request like {"tool": "get_order", "args": [1004]}; your code runs the function and feeds the result back.

The right panel shows the state dictionary changing and the equivalent LangGraph code.

lessons.title: Byte-Pair Encoding from scratch
lessons.blurb: The algorithm behind GPT-style tokenizers, in under 30 lines of Python.

pages.html:
Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) learns a vocabulary from data. Start with the bytes of the text as tokens. Repeat: find the most frequent pair of neighbouring tokens, give that pair a new id, and replace every occurrence. After k merges you have k new tokens, and common words or word-pieces have become single tokens.

pages.h: Keep hot data close, split big data up

lessons.title: Rate limits, retries and queues
lessons.blurb: Protect a service from floods, retry safely, and make repeated requests harmless.

pages.h: Things fail, so design for it
pages.html:
• Rate limiting protects a service from one noisy client. A token bucket holds up to capacity tokens and refills at rate per second; each request spends one; an empty bucket means "429 Too Many Requests". It allows short bursts but caps the long-run rate.
  • Retries fix temporary failures, but retrying instantly makes an overloaded service worse. Use exponential backoff (wait 0.5, 1, 2, 4... seconds, up to a cap) with jitter (a random fraction) so thousands of clients do not retry together.
  • Idempotency

    This is an excerpt. The full lesson continues in the course.

lessons.title: Layout, contrast and accessibility
lessons.blurb: Contrast ratios, click-target size and a type scale: visual design you can compute.

pages.h: Make the important thing obvious and readable by everyone
pages.html:
• Visual hierarchy: size, weight, colour and space tell the eye what to read first. One main action per screen; related things grouped closely; unrelated things separated by space.
  • Contrast: WCAG asks for a ratio of at least 4.5 : 1 for normal text and 3 : 1 for large text. The ratio comes from relative luminance: convert each colour channel from sRGB to linear light, then L = 0.2126 R + 0.7152 G + 0.0722 B, and ratio = (Llight + 0.05) / (Ldark + 0.05).
  • Never rely on colour alone: add labels, icons or patterns, because about 1 in 12 men have a colour-vision difference.

pages.h: Test early, with a few people; experiment later, with many
pages.html:
• Usability test: 5 to 8 people do realistic tasks while you watch (think aloud). Each person finds a share p (about 0.31 on average) of the problems, so the chance that at least one of n people meets a given problem is 1 - (1 - p)^n: 5 people find about 85% of problems, and after that it is better to fix and re-test than to add more people.
  • UI experiment (A/B): when you need to know if version B converts better, split real traffic randomly. Compare two rates with a two-proportion z-test: pooled rate p, standard error sqrt(p(1-p)(1/nA + 1/nB)), z = (pB - pA) / se

pages.h: Five lines that train every neural network

for epoch in range(epochs):

        loss = loss_fn(pred, yb)     #    how wrong
        optimizer.zero_grad()        # 3. clear old gradients (they accumulate!)

        optimizer.step()             # 5. update the weights

lessons.title: Detection and segmentation building blocks
lessons.blurb: IoU, non-max suppression and the Dice score: the maths inside object detectors and segmenters.

pages.html:
• Classification: one label per image. Detection: a box and a label for every object (YOLO, Faster R-CNN). Segmentation: a label for every pixel (U-Net, Mask R-CNN).
  • IoU (intersection over union) scores how well two boxes overlap: area of overlap / area of union, from 0 (disjoint) to 1 (identical). A detection is "correct" when its IoU with a true box is at least 0.5.
  • Non-max suppression (NMS): detectors output many overlapping boxes for one object. Keep the highest-scoring box, throw away any other box that overlaps it by more than a threshold, and repeat with what is left.
  • Dice and IoU

pages.h: Every token decides whom to listen to
pages.html:
Self-attention lets each token build its new vector as a weighted mix of all tokens. Each token produces a query Q (what am I looking for), a key K (what do I offer) and a value V (what I pass on). The weights are softmax(Q KT / sqrt(d)); the output is weights @ V. Dividing by sqrt(d) keeps the numbers from growing with the vector size.

lessons.title: LoRA: tune a tiny adapter, freeze the giant
lessons.blurb: Write the low-rank trick yourself: parameter savings, an adapter that starts as the base model, merging and adapter-only training.

pages.h: The change in a weight matrix can be small in rank
pages.html:
Full fine-tuning updates every weight W (a d_in x d_out matrix) of the model and needs gradients and optimizer memory for all of them. LoRA observes that the change needed is usually low-rank, so it freezes W and learns delta = A @ B with A: d_in x r and B: r x d_out and a small rank r (4 to 64). The layer computes y = x W + (alpha / r) (x A) B.

This is an excerpt. The full lesson continues in the course.

lessons.title: Quantisation and memory
lessons.blurb: How many gigabytes a model needs, and how int8 and 4-bit weights shrink it.

pages.h: A model is a pile of numbers; the number format decides its size
pages.html:
• Memory of the weights = parameters x bytes per parameter. A 7-billion-parameter model is 14 GB in 16-bit (2 bytes), 7 GB in 8-bit and about 3.5 GB in 4-bit.
  • Training memory is much larger: with mixed-precision Adam you need roughly 16 bytes per trainable parameter (weights, gradients and two optimizer moments) plus activations. LoRA trains few parameters, so almost all of that disappears; QLoRA also shrinks the frozen base to 4-bit.
  • Quantisation maps floats to a few integer levels: scale = max|x| / 127, q = round(x / scale), and x ~ q * scale. The error per weight is at most scale / 2

    This is an excerpt. The full lesson continues in the course.

pages.h: Did tuning help, or did it just feel better?

• Write the test cases before you train and never train on them. Include hard and unusual inputs.

lessons.title: Config, containers and the CI gate
lessons.blurb: Read settings from the environment, understand Docker layer caching, and block a bad release automatically.

pages.h: The same code must run everywhere
pages.html:
• Configuration lives outside the code, in environment variables (PORT, MODEL_PATH, secrets). The same image then runs in development, staging and production with different settings. Parse and validate the settings at start-up and fail fast if one is missing.
  • Docker layers: each instruction creates a cached layer. When a file changes, that layer and every layer after it is rebuilt. So copy requirements.txt and install dependencies before copying your source code: editing code then reuses the slow install layer.
  • CI gate: on every change CI runs tests and a model gate

    This is an excerpt. The full lesson continues in the course.

lessons.title: APIs, pagination and retries
lessons.blurb: Build query strings, walk every page and survive temporary failures.

pages.html:
• Prefer the API. Many sites expose JSON endpoints (open the browser's Network tab). They are faster, cleaner and often allowed explicitly.
  • Query strings: parameters are encoded after a ?: urllib.parse.urlencode({"q": "a b&c"}) gives q=a+b%26c. Never build them by joining strings.
  • Pagination: a response contains a page of items and how to get the next page (a page number, an offset, or an opaque cursor). Loop until there is no next page, and keep a maximum page count so a bug cannot loop forever.
  • Retries with backoff

lessons.title: Analysing a test and its pitfalls
lessons.blurb: An interval, a Bayesian probability, and why peeking and many metrics create false winners.

pages.h: A p-value is not the whole story
pages.html:
• Report the effect with an interval: "B raised conversion by 3.0 points (95% CI 0.2 to 5.8)", not just "p = 0.04". The interval shows how big and how uncertain.
  • Bayesian view: start from a flat prior, update with the data, and get the probability that B is better than A directly. With s successes in n, the posterior of the rate is Beta(1 + s, 1 + n - s). Sample from both posteriors and count how often B beats A.
  • Peeking: a fixed-sample test is valid only if you look once

    This is an excerpt. The full lesson continues in the course.

lessons.title: Recommenders and ranking metrics
lessons.blurb: Item-item collaborative filtering, and scoring a ranked list with precision, recall, MAP and NDCG.

pages.h: People who liked this also liked...
pages.html:
Collaborative filtering recommends using the behaviour of many users. Item-item: two items are similar if the same people rated or bought them (cosine similarity between their columns of the user-item matrix). To recommend for a user, score each item they have not seen by its similarity to the items they liked and take the top k. It needs no information about the items themselves; its weakness is the cold start (new users and new items have no history). Real systems add content features and learned embeddings (matrix factorisation, two-tower models).

This is an excerpt. The full lesson continues in the course.

pages.h: Boring maths that must be exactly right
pages.html:
• Invoice: subtotal = sum of quantity x unit price; apply the discount to the subtotal; tax is charged on the discounted amount; total = taxable amount + tax; amount due = total - deposit already paid. Show every line.
  • Payment terms: "net 30" means due 30 days after the invoice date. A late fee (for example 1.5% per month, after a short grace period) is stated in the contract before work starts.
  • Milestones: split the fee (30% to start, 40% on the first delivery, 30% on handover). Money is stored in cents as integers so rounding cannot invent or lose a cent; share out the leftover cents to the largest fractional parts.

pages.h: Run it like a small business

• Utilisation: only part of your working time is billable (sales, admin, learning and gaps take the rest). If you want to earn 6,000 a month at 40 an hour you need 150 billable hours; at 60% utilisation that is 250 working hours, about 58 a week. Raise the rate before you raise the hours.
  • Client lifetime value (LTV) = average monthly revenue x months the client stays (x margin). Customer acquisition cost (CAC) = what it cost to win them. Payback = CAC / monthly margin. Repeat clients and referrals have CAC near zero: delivering well is your marketing.

lessons.title: Batching and speculative decoding

pages.html:
Static batching groups requests and waits for the longest one to finish; short requests leave idle slots. Continuous batching refills a slot the moment its request ends, so slots are busy nearly all the time. Servers such as vLLM do this by default.

lessons.title: Audio, spectrograms and speech accuracy
lessons.blurb: Turn a waveform into an image of sound, and score a transcript.

pages.html:
A sound is a long list of numbers (16,000 per second for speech). Models do not read it raw. They cut it into short overlapping frames (for example 25 ms every 10 ms), multiply each frame by a smooth window (Hann) so its edges do not create false frequencies, and take a Fourier transform: how much energy there is at each frequency. Stacking the frames gives a spectrogram: time across, pitch up.

This is an excerpt. The full lesson continues in the course.

lessons.title: Multimodal pipelines: cost, OCR and latency
lessons.blurb: What a picture costs in tokens, and how long a voice reply takes.

pages.html:
Pictures cost tokens. Many vision-language APIs split an image into 512-pixel tiles, charge a fixed number of tokens per tile plus a small base, and shrink very large images first. A big screenshot can cost as much as a page of text; knowing the formula lets you resize or crop sensibly.
